1.note: Here David is speaking as if his **heart** were something that could be **made steadfast**. He means that he has become determined and committed to praising God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made myself steadfast]

The expression **My heart is made steadfast** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I have made my heart steadfast]

The word translated as **glory** could be: (1) a reference to all of David’s strength. Alternate translation: [indeed, with all that I am] or (2) translated as the very similar word for “liver.” In this case, it would be understood as functioning very much like **heart** in the first part of the verse, and also stand for the place in the body where a person’s will and emotions are. Either way you translate it, the meaning is very similar. Alternate translation: [indeed, with my liver] or [indeed, with my entire will]

2.note: See how you translated the similar phrases in Psalm 57:8.

David is speaking of his **lyre and harp** as if they were living things that could wake up from sleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will start making music with my lyre and harp]

David is speaking of **the dawn** as if it were a living thing that could be awakened. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will play them before the sun comes up]

3.note: These two phrases **I will thank you, Yahweh, among the peoples** and **I will make music to you among the nations** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I will thank you and make music to you, Yahweh, among the peoples of other nations]

4.note: These two phrases **your covenant faithfulness is great from above the heavens** and **your trustworthiness above the clouds** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [For your covenant faithfulness and your trustworthiness are higher than the heavens]

Here David is speaking of God’s covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness as if they were physical things that could extend **above the heavens** and **above the clouds**. He means that God’s faithfulness and trustworthiness are immeasurably great. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [For your covenant faithfulness is better than any human covenant faithfulness, and your trustworthiness is better than any human trustworthiness]

David is using **great from above the heavens** as a common expression of his culture to mean “higher than the heavens” or “greater than the heavens.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For your covenant faithfulness is higher than the heavens]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way that you faithfully love us]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your trustworthiness is great from above the clouds]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trustworthiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the amount that we can trust you is]

5.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־שָׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: See how you translated the similar phrases in Psalm 57:5

5.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־שָׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: Here David is speaking of God as if he were a person who could be **exalted**, or lifted, above the heavens. David means that God should be recognized and praised as being greater than anything in the heavens. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Show how great you are, God, greater than the heavens, and show your glory to everyone on earth]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may your glory be exalted over all the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and how glorious you are over all the earth]

6.q: לְ֭מַעַן יֵחָלְצ֣וּ⁠ן יְדִידֶ֑י⁠ךָ הוֹשִׁ֖יעָ⁠ה יְמִֽינְ⁠ךָ֣ וַ⁠עֲנֵֽ⁠נִי
6.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the purpose, **So that your beloved ones may be rescued**, after the request, **save with your right hand and answer me**. Alternate translation: [Save with your right hand and answer me so that your beloved ones may be rescued]

The expression **may be rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [So that you rescue your beloved ones]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please save with your right hand and answer me]

Here David is using **hand** to represent Yahweh’s power or strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your ability] or [by your strength]

Here, **answer me** represents “do what I have been requesting.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and do what I have been requesting]

7.q: אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ דִּבֶּ֥ר בְּ⁠קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ אֶעְלֹ֥זָה אֲחַלְּקָ֥ה שְׁכֶ֑ם וְ⁠עֵ֖מֶק סֻכּ֣וֹת אֲמַדֵּֽד
7.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:6

Here, **in his holiness** could either represent (1) the basis or source of God’s authority when he speaks. Alternate translation: [by his holy authority] or [from his holy nature] or (2) the holy place where God was thought to dwell. Alternate translation: [from his holy place] or [from his sanctuary]

By **I shall divide Shechem**, God means that he will divide the land where Shechem is located. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I shall divide the land surrounding Shechem]

By **the Valley of Succoth**, God means the territory or region around the Valley of Succoth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and measure out the territory of the Valley of Succoth]

By **measure out**, God means “measure out for my people to possess.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for my people make portions of]

8.q: לִ֤⁠י גִלְעָ֨ד ׀ לִ֤⁠י מְנַשֶּׁ֗ה וְ֭⁠אֶפְרַיִם מָע֣וֹז רֹאשִׁ֑⁠י יְ֝הוּדָ֗ה מְחֹקְקִֽ⁠י
8.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:7

God is using **To me is** as a common expression of his culture to mean “belongs to me” or “is mine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Gilead belongs to me; Manasseh belongs to me]

Here God is speaking of **Ephraim** as if it were **the protection of my head**, meaning a helmet that protects a warrior in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the people of Ephraim are my warriors]

Here God is speaking of **Judah** as if it were a **scepter**. He means that God rules through the kings of the tribe of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I rule through the kings of the tribe of Judah]

God is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Judah is my scepter]

9.q: מוֹאָ֤ב ׀ סִ֬יר רַחְצִ֗⁠י עַל־אֱ֭דוֹם אַשְׁלִ֣יךְ נַעֲלִ֑⁠י עֲלֵֽי־פְ֝לֶ֗שֶׁת אֶתְרוֹעָֽע
9.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:8.

Here God is speaking of **Moab** as if it were **a tub for my washing**. He means that the people of Moab will serve him in a menial way, like servants who bring a basin for washing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Moab are like servants who wash my feet]

Here God is speaking of **Edom** as if it were a servant who removes his sandals. This image shows that Edom will be completely defeated and will serve Israel in the most menial ways. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Edom are like servants who remove my sandals]

10.q: מִ֣י יֹ֭בִלֵ⁠נִי עִ֣יר מִבְצָ֑ר מִ֖י נָחַ֣⁠נִי עַד־אֱדֽוֹם
10.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:9.

10.q: מִ֣י יֹ֭בִלֵ⁠נִי עִ֣יר מִבְצָ֑ר מִ֖י נָחַ֣⁠נִי עַד־אֱדֽוֹם
10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Who will lead me to Edom** before the information about **Who will bring me into the strong city**. Alternate translation: [Who will lead me to Edom? Who will bring me into the strong city?]

David assumes that readers will know that **the strong city** refers to a fortified city in Edom, likely its capital. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Who will bring me into the strong capital city of Edom?]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only God can bring me into the strong city.]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only God can lead me to Edom.]

11.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:10.

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God, it seems that you have rejected us!]

12.q: הָֽבָ⁠ה־לָּ֣⁠נוּ עֶזְרָ֣ת מִ⁠צָּ֑ר וְ֝⁠שָׁ֗וְא תְּשׁוּעַ֥ת אָדָֽם
12.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:11.

David is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means enemies in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [against all of our enemies]

Here the word **and** introduces not an additional action but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [since futility is the deliverance of man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **futility**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [since expecting humans to save us is futile]

David is using this possessive form **the deliverance of man** to mean deliverance that comes from human beings. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [any deliverance by human beings]

13.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 60:12.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [we will succeed valiantly]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **will trample** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is God who will defeat the enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and it is he who will trample our adversaries]

Here David is speaking of God in the third person as **he** even though he has been addressing God directly in the previous verses. This may be to give encouragement to the Israelites who are listening. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person to maintain the direct address. Alternate translation: [and you, you will trample our adversaries]

Here David is speaking of God as if he were a warrior who would **trample** the enemies underfoot. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this plainly. Alternate translation: [and he, he will completely defeat our adversaries]
